topic_tag: island basket weaving and a marketing board
passage: In 1952 a state marketing board began buying the reed baskets that households on a small fishing island had woven for generations. Until then the baskets had carried the catch to the island's smokehouses. The board's buyers sent them to city department stores, which displayed them beside lamps and flowerpots in their furnishing departments and priced one at five times what a fish basket cost on the quay. By 1975 the same households were weaving about as many baskets as they always had, while the crews had gone over to plastic crates. Visiting the island in 1975, one folklorist concluded that the board's purchases had ______ the craft.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: Baskets made to carry fish ended up among city furnishings while the crews switched to crates, so the purchases "repurposed" the craft, turning it to a new use. "Rekindled" fails because households wove about as many baskets as they always had; the craft never lapsed. "Professionalized" fails because the same households did the weaving. "Petrified" fails because the passage reports a change in what the baskets were for, not a freezing of their form.

topic_tag: a valley's role in an early forestry service
passage: A state forestry service founded in 1911 managed the timber of a mountainous province, and one of its fourteen districts was a narrow valley. The service had money to survey only one district, and in 1912 its foresters counted and measured every tree on the valley's slopes. For the next thirty years each district's yearly cutting limit was set in proportion to its area from a single table of timber per acre, a table revised only when the valley was counted again. One historian argues that, from 1911 to 1940, the valley was above all the service's ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: Every district's cutting limit came from a table built on the valley's count and updated only when the valley was recounted, so the valley stood for all fourteen as the service's "proxy." "Prototype" fails because nothing was built in the valley and then copied; only its figures were used. "Outpost" fails because the passage describes a survey, not a remote station. "Reservoir" fails because the service took figures from the valley, not a supply it held back and drew on.

topic_tag: a minor character's function in a novel
passage: A nineteenth-century novel follows two sisters who inherit a country estate, and the family's gardener speaks fewer lines than any other recurring character. In the second chapter he plants a bed of white roses beneath the elder sister's window, the following spring tears every one of them out, and in the last chapter quietly replants them. The narrator, who explains every other character's motives at length, offers no motive for any of these acts, and neither sister ever remarks on the roses. In an often-cited essay, one critic calls the gardener the novel's ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The gardener plants, uproots and replants the same roses, and the narrator, who explains everyone else, never explains him, so he is the novel's "puzzle." "Prism" fails because the story is not told from his point of view. "Pivot" fails because his acts go unnoticed and change nothing in the plot. "Pawn" fails because no one directs him; he acts on his own, for reasons no one gives.

topic_tag: an eighteenth-century map of a kingdom
passage: In 1790 a country surveyor published a map of the kingdom that went through eleven printings in twenty years. Rival maps copied their coastlines and roads from older charts, errors and all. The surveyor spent eleven summers on the kingdom's roads with a chain and a brass quadrant, plotting each town himself. When the government checked his sheets with better instruments sixty years later, few of his distances were off by more than a mile. Comparing it with other maps of its day, one historian describes the surveyor's map as, above all, ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: Where rivals copied old errors, the surveyor spent eleven summers measuring roads and plotting towns himself, and a later survey found his distances nearly exact, so the map was "rigorous." "Prescient" fails because the map recorded what existed accurately rather than anticipating what would come. "Provincial" fails because his measurements covered the whole kingdom. "Portable" fails because nothing is said about the map's size or how it was carried.

topic_tag: a weavers' hall in a market town
passage: In 1871 the hand-loom weavers of a hill district pooled their dues to buy a hall in the market town. Over the next decades the mill owners bought the market, the bank, and most council seats, and turned each against home weaving. The weavers' old price agreement and apprentice rules, struck from the town's books in 1880, were still read out and obeyed at monthly meetings in the hall. The deed needed every member's signature to sell, and the owners' offers for it, made almost yearly, ended only in 1919. For the next half century, one historian has argued, the hall served the district's weavers chiefly as their ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The owners took over every other institution, the weavers' repealed rules lived on only inside the hall, and the hall withstood yearly attempts to buy it; combining these shows it was the place the weavers held against the owners, their "stronghold." "Springboard" fails because the weavers were keeping their trade's rules, not using the hall to leave the trade. "Showpiece" fails because the hall's value lay in being held against the owners, not in being displayed. "Switchboard" fails because nothing in the passage passes through the hall from one party to another.

topic_tag: a truce between two river towns
passage: For most of the eighteenth century, two towns on opposite banks of a salmon river tore down each other's fish weirs whenever the run was good. In 1790 the two councils signed a truce at a feast on the bridge, and they renewed it with the same toasts every spring until 1815. In no year of the twenty-five, the magistrates' books show, were fewer weirs cut on either bank than in the decades before. Neither council fined a single man for crossing to the far bank, and the feast grew larger every year. Writing a century later, one historian called the truce between the towns from 1790 to 1815 ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The truce was signed and toasted every year, while weir-cutting never fell below its old rate in any year and no one was punished; combining these shows the truce existed in name only, so it was "token." "Tacit" fails because the truce was signed openly. "Tactical" fails because a truce made for an aim still holds while the aim lasts, and this one never held in any year. "Unilateral" fails because neither town held back.

topic_tag: a marsh above a harbor town
passage: Above a harbor town, a river crosses six miles of reedy marsh, and below the marsh the lower river runs past the town's quays to the bay. The marsh floor is hard clay laced with tidal creeks that empty into the bay a mile from town. When the river rises past a certain height, only the water above that level pours over a low bank into the marsh, and the creeks are back to their usual level by morning. In floods the lower river past the quays stays at its ordinary height. One hydrologist has concluded that the marsh serves the lower river as a kind of ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: Only the excess water above a set level leaves the river, runs across the hard clay and out to the bay by the creeks within a night, and the lower river is spared the flood; combining these shows the marsh carries off surplus water, so it is "a kind of spillway." "Sponge" fails because the clay floor takes nothing in and the creeks are back to normal by morning. "Sieve" fails because the marsh changes how much water reaches the lower river, not what is in it. "Seedbed" fails because nothing in the passage begins life in the marsh.

topic_tag: the first recording of a ballad
passage: In 1928 a record company made the first recording of an old ballad from the hill counties, about a ferryman drowned in a flood. In the hill counties it had been sung only in church at funerals, and its last verse was a prayer for the ferryman's soul. The record kept the hill singers' hard voices and fiddle, replaced the prayer with a verse naming the river and the year of the flood, and was sold to the dance halls, where it was played between reels. One folklorist has argued that the 1928 recording had ______ the ballad.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The record took a funeral hymn, removed its prayer, and sent it to the dance halls, so the recording "secularized" the ballad. "Standardized" fails because the passage concerns where and why the ballad was sung, not the number of versions. "Sweetened" fails because the record kept the hill singers' hard sound. "Unearthed" fails because the ballad was already sung at every funeral in the hill counties.

topic_tag: an island port held by an empire
passage: In 1560 an empire seized a small island port at the mouth of a strait on the main sea route to its eastern provinces. At the island the strait narrows to a channel one ship wide, close beneath the harbor. Every merchant ship's master went ashore at the island's harbor office and returned with a stamped paper before sailing on, and the empire's patrol at the strait's far end turned back any ship without one. The treasury's ledgers show that the office's receipts paid for the empire's whole navy in those waters. For the next century, one historian has argued, the empire valued the island chiefly as its ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: Ships could only use the strait with a paper bought at the island's harbor office, and those receipts funded a navy, so the empire valued the island as its "tollgate." "Storehouse" fails because ships sailed on with their cargo after getting the paper. "Watchtower" fails because the island's role was charging ships for passage, not watching for enemies. "Trophy" fails because the island produced large revenues.

topic_tag: mountain monastery's role between two valleys
passage: For six centuries a small monastery stood at the top of the only pass between two mountain valleys, each ruled by its own lord. In time the eastern lord grew rich enough to want the western valley's pastures. The monks owned the high grazing land on the pass, chose each abbot from western families, and had the bishop's backing in every quarrel. Whenever the eastern lord gathered men to march west, the abbot gathered tenants and the bishop's letters, and for two centuries the lord never judged the march worth the cost. In a history of the pass, one scholar described the monastery as, above all, the region's ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: Each time the eastern lord built up force, the monastery built up an answering force of its own, tenants and church backing, and the march never came, so the monastery held the balance: it was the region's "counterweight." "Checkpoint" fails because the lord is deterred by what the monastery could raise, not stopped at a gate; "broker" fails because the monastery answers one side's threat instead of arranging terms; "custodian" fails because it holds its own land and keeps nothing in trust for anyone.

topic_tag: a coastal trading house and a river town's grain trade
passage: In 1782 a trading house from the coast opened an office in a river town where farmers from the surrounding district had long sold their grain. Over the next decade it bought the harvest of nearly every farm in the district at the town's scales and leased both of the town's warehouses. By the late 1790s harvests were as large as ever, the millers downriver were paying more for the town's grain each autumn, and each year's price matched the figure the house's agent posted on the market door. One economic historian has argued that by 1800 the house had ______ the town's grain trade.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The house bought nearly all the grain and all the storage, and afterward the price rose with steady harvests to whatever its agent posted, so it controlled supply and price: it "cornered" the town's grain trade. "Awakened" fails because farmers had long sold grain in the town; "bankrolled" fails because the house bought the grain itself rather than funding others; "coordinated" fails because, holding the harvest and both warehouses, it took the trade over rather than organizing other dealers.

topic_tag: a composer's use of a folk tune in a symphony
passage: In 1907 a composer built one movement of his first symphony on a folk tune he had heard in a fishing village. The village fiddlers played it as thirty-two bars, repeated for as long as the dancing lasted, and its first eight bars were the part every child in the village could hum. In the symphony the orchestra plays the phrase the children knew, note for note and at the fiddlers' own speed, over and over until the movement ends. Comparing the symphony with the village version, one critic observed that the composer had ______ the tune.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The phrase the children knew is the tune's first eight bars of thirty-two, and the symphony repeats that phrase alone to the end, so the composer "clipped" the tune: he cut it short. "Braided" fails because nothing else is joined to it; the movement just repeats the phrase; "animated" fails because it keeps the fiddlers' own speed; "cleansed" fails because the phrase keeps every note.

topic_tag: a hospital trustee's role
passage: For most of the 1960s a retired surgeon sat on the nine-member board of trustees of a county hospital. The hospital depended on a yearly grant from the state health department and on a road the county commissioners maintained to its door. Each spring for the whole decade the trustees settled in closed session on what to ask of both, and she then spent several weeks in the capital and the county seat. The board's minutes for each summer record it debating the officials' replies, which she read into the record herself. In an oral history recorded decades later, one fellow trustee called her the board's ______ during those years.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The trustees decided what to ask, she then spent weeks where the state and county officials sat, and the replies the board debated came back through her, so she was its "envoy," the representative it sent to outside parties. "Gatekeeper" fails because she did not decide what the board considered; the trustees settled the requests and debated the replies. "Figurehead" fails because weeks of dealing with officials was real work, not a title. "Holdout" fails because she carried requests the trustees had agreed on together.

topic_tag: a harvest procession over fifty years
passage: For centuries the villages of one mountain valley marked the end of the olive harvest with a night procession, led by singers, from the church to the presses. In 1951 a national law added the procession to a list of forty "living monuments" of the country. From then on the state closed the route to traffic on each harvest night, paid to repair the presses and lanterns, and sent an inspector every year to confirm that route, verses, and singers matched the description filed in 1951, while neighboring valleys' customs lapsed. Writing in 1990, one folklorist concluded that the changes of the previous fifty years had ______ the custom.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: A national law listed the procession as a monument, the state funded its upkeep, and an inspector held it each year to its 1951 form, so the changes had "enshrined" the custom, preserving it as something honored and protected. "Democratized" fails because the singers had to match the 1951 description, so participation was not opened up. "Dramatized" fails because the event was held to its old form, not restaged as a show. "Harmonized" fails because each village's procession was kept as described rather than made uniform.

topic_tag: an outbreak in a stand of oaks
passage: Since 1985 foresters have surveyed a stand of oaks on a dry ridge every summer, and in the early 1990s an outbreak struck it. The outbreak was a root fungus, which rots the thick roots that anchor an oak while its trunk stays sound and its crown stays in full leaf. As the rot spread, the surveys measured the oaks leaning a little further each year. By 2005 they recorded open ground where the stand had been, with the trunks lying across it, each still attached to a rotted mass of roots. Summing up three decades of surveys, one forester wrote that the outbreak had ______ the oaks.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The fungus rotted only the anchoring roots, so the full-grown trees leaned further each year until they lay on the ground, roots rotted through: the outbreak had "felled" the oaks. "Dwarfed" fails because the trees were full-size, with sound trunks and full crowns, when they came down. "Defoliated" fails because the fungus attacked roots and left the crowns in leaf. "Honeycombed" fails because the trunks stayed sound; the damage was below ground.

topic_tag: a pamphlet and a tenants' movement
passage: In 1882 a forty-page pamphlet on the rights of tenant farmers appeared in one rural province, the same year a tenants' movement formed there. Its pages repeated arguments already made in every newspaper in the province, and copies found in members' homes decades later are mostly uncut beyond the first few leaves. The movement printed it in runs of twenty thousand, members sold copies for a penny at fairs and markets, and the proceeds paid the rent of the halls where its branches met and the fees of lawyers who defended evicted tenants. Looking back, one historian called the pamphlet the movement's ______ in its first decade.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: Its arguments were familiar and its pages largely unopened, while huge penny runs paid for halls and lawyers, so the pamphlet was the movement's "fundraiser." "Handbook" fails because its pages held arguments, not procedures, and most copies were never opened past the start. "Gospel" fails because a pamphlet repeating commonplace arguments, left unread, was not the movement's revered authority. "Foil" fails because the movement printed and sold it itself rather than arguing against it.

topic_tag: a flood in a farming valley
passage: In the spring of 1936 a flood swept the length of a narrow farming valley, where a river had run for centuries between orchards and cornfields to a rocky gorge at the valley's lower end. Driven by a gale, a wall of water a few feet high crossed the valley in less than an hour and was gone by evening. Surveyors later found every orchard tree and cornstalk still rooted in soil the water had barely disturbed, and photographs from the ridge show the valley floor striped in the direction the water had run. Revisiting the valley a decade later, one geographer wrote that the flood had ______ it.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: A fast, shallow wall of water left trees and stalks rooted in undisturbed soil yet showed from above as stripes running with the current, so it had laid them over: the flood had "flattened" the valley's growth. "Dammed" fails because the water was gone within hours. "Gouged" fails because the soil was barely disturbed. "Emptied" fails because the trees and crops stayed rooted where they grew.

topic_tag: a railway town and a port city
passage: A small town lies forty miles north of a large port city, on a railway line opened in 1890. After a naval raid on the port in 1914, the army chose the town's station as the place from which troops could reach the city's docks within an hour. Through the 1920s three regiments took turns there, drilling all day on the old fairground and going to the city only for alerts and exercises, and the town's shops lived largely on the soldiers' pay. By 1930, one regional planner observed, the town had in effect become the city's ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The army placed regiments at the town so they could reach the port's docks within an hour, and they trained there and went to the city only when called, so the town had become the city's "garrison," the base of the force that defended it. "Dormitory" fails because the soldiers spent their days in the town and went to the city only on alert, rather than working there daily. "Getaway" fails because those arriving were stationed troops, not city people seeking leisure. "Granary" fails because the town lived on the soldiers' pay, not on grain.

topic_tag: a village boatyard's role on its coast
passage: In 1871 the fishermen of a small harbor village on a rocky coast pooled their savings to open a boatyard. Every hull it sold cost a little more than its timber and labor, and the yard kept the difference apart from its own profits. After the storm of 1893 sank fourteen boats, it paid for fourteen new hulls, each handed at no charge to a family that had lost one, and by 1921 every boat lost on that coast had been rebuilt this way. Looking back on its first fifty years, one historian argued that the yard had served the coast above all as its ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: Every buyer paid a little extra into a sum the yard kept apart, and that sum rebuilt the boats of whoever suffered a loss, so the yard served as the coast's "insurer." "Lender" fails because the new hulls were handed over at no charge and were never repaid; "memory" fails because the passage describes money held against losses, not a record of the coast's past; "incubator" fails because the yard restored existing fishing families rather than raising up new enterprises that went off on their own.

topic_tag: a newspaper theater critic's record
passage: For thirty-one years a single critic wrote the weekly theater column of a city newspaper. By her last decade she had reviewed well over two thousand productions. Her reviews from those years shrink to a single paragraph, and the word she used most often in them was "familiar." Several plays she dismissed that way were hailed as fresh by younger critics in the same season and ran for years. Having read the full run of her reviews, one theater historian described the critic as ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: After thousands of productions, her reviews dwindled and she dismissed as familiar plays that others found fresh, so she had become "jaded." "Judicious" fails because the plays she waved off succeeded, so her verdicts did not reflect sound judgment; "mercurial" fails because her response was the same dismissal again and again; "insistent" fails because she was pressing no demand, only losing interest.

topic_tag: a river port's customs inspector
passage: From 1878 to 1901 a single inspector examined the cargo landed at a small river port for the customs service. Captains complained that unloading at his port took twice as long as at the larger ports on the river. His reports note differences between the crates and the ships' papers as small as a bolt of cloth a yard short, and when his successor checked twenty years of them against the shippers' own invoices, he found them accurate to the last item. Reading his reports a century later, one historian described the inspector as ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: Slow unloading, tiny discrepancies recorded, and reports later found exact to the last item together show he was "meticulous." "Naive" fails because he checked the crates against the ships' papers rather than accepting them; "lenient" fails because the passage reports how closely he checked, not how mildly he punished; "incorruptible" fails because nothing concerns bribes or attempts to sway him.

topic_tag: a printed ballad passed on by ear
passage: In 1790 a port-town printer sold a ballad about a young sailor who deserts his ship and drowns in a storm on his way home. A century later, folklorists collected it from singers who had learned it by ear. In nearly every version, once the storm rises, the song goes on with the verses of a farm girl's lament sold by the same printer, his name now set into its lines as her lost sweetheart's. The two songs share a tune and a rhyme scheme, and no singer could say where one ended. Comparing the versions, one folklorist concluded that a hundred years of singing had ______ the ballad.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The singers joined the ballad to a second printed song so smoothly that no one could find the seam, so singing had "merged" the ballad with another. "Mangled" fails because the joined song is seamless and makes sense, with the sailor's name fitted into the lament; "mellowed" fails because the sailor's fate is not softened: grief is added to it; "moralized" fails because the added verses mourn rather than teach a lesson.
